name: Vera Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and fit fire doors on apartment building sites. A vocational trade certificate got me into carpentry, and now I measure frames, hang doors and test the closers with the supervisor. I like a door that shuts cleanly; carrying a heavy leaf up unfinished stairs wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a shop, our children are grown, and retirement is in sight if the money works. My pay is typical for the trade, we have about three months of expenses saved and some similar contractors are nearby. I use AI now and then for long specifications, but I trust an actual door test; I hope to finish regular work around 66 if our figures allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quicker fire-door checklist is welcome, but somebody still has to fit the frame square and test the closer. I would carry on with the crew rather than make a fuss over modest software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 58 and on the usual carpenter's wage, with about three months of expenses saved. My partner works at a shop, our children are grown, and I hope to finish regular site work around 66 if our retirement figures support it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting fire doors on the apartment site and check each closer with the building supervisor. This month my partner and I will gather our retirement statements and household bills to see how far our planned working years need to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the present job, though I want the retirement numbers on paper. The checklist will save me a few minutes, not change whether the door shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a checklist miss a door problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the last floor I checked the door by hand. The fire-door closer passed the printed tick box but the door caught on a raised threshold. I planed the edge and tested the shut again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the retirement check include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would list both expected retirement incomes and the regular household bills. That is a check, not a decision to leave work early.

say: **Fire-door fitting** still needs physical closer and threshold tests.
A quicker **checklist** leaves the site job mostly as it is.
think: My **usual trade wage** looks steady and our children are grown.
Three months of **expenses saved** makes retirement figures worth checking before setting an exit date.
do: **Fit** apartment fire doors and test closers with building supervisor.
**Compare** retirement statements with household bills this month.
feel: **Calm** about current wages, thoughtful about later affordability.
S0.quote: The fire-door closer passed the printed tick box but the door caught on a raised threshold.
fieldNote: She catches a **raised threshold** through a physical door test after the checklist said pass.
Retirement around **66 is conditional** on statements and bills; gathering numbers does not mean early exit.

steps.text: Fit apartment fire doors and test closers with supervisor
Compare retirement statements with household bills this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site crew AI can order hinges and book inspections before a robot can hang a heavy fire door. The office still needs a fitter to say whether the closer works on the actual floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid door work seems safe while the software takes desk tasks, but a wrong order could send us home early. There are some other contractors nearby, yet at 58 I would rather keep reliable days with this team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll mark the hinge sizes used on the next two apartment floors and compare them with the office order. If a new AI scheduling screen is adopted and a colleague shows it working on real door jobs, I'll learn its correction controls on paid time before relying on the next delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the order desk moving faster than the site, with my own wage still looking safe. I do not need to be first to try every screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hinge order is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office the hinge size and room number before the truck is loaded. A wrong hinge can hold a fire door open when the building needs it to shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What proof would make you try the scheduling screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a colleague to show a corrected order from an actual floor and paid time to practise. If the firm offers only a brochure, I'll keep sending measurements from my notebook.

say: **AI orders** may change before robots hang fire doors.
Fitters must **verify closers and hinges** on the real floor.
think: My **door-fitting wage** looks safe for now.
Wrong **hinge orders** could shorten a day, though nearby contractors give some options.
do: **Compare** hinges used on two apartment floors with office orders.
**Learn** adopted scheduling corrections on paid time after colleague shows real job.
feel: **Uneasy** about faster office orders while work stays reliable.
S1.quote: A wrong hinge can hold a fire door open when the building needs it to shut.
fieldNote: She will learn **new AI controls** only after an adopted tool is proven on a real floor and paid practice exists.
She names a possible **short day**, but expects her own work and wage to remain stable in the slower change.

steps.text: Compare hinges on two apartment floors with office orders
Learn adopted AI scheduling corrections on paid time after real-job demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could plan the door schedule, then capable robots around 2031 could fit the frames. I want to see paid crew numbers before a machine is counted as a replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 63 when robots can do site fitting, three years before the age when I hope to stop. If the contractor cuts my door days then, the wage gap could be hard to cover. Three months of savings and some local jobs may not bridge a fire-door wage gap to an affordable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the contractor for the door crew plan and paid training options, then review retirement statements with my partner. If the firm cuts my shifts, I'll apply only to a posted local fire-door inspection vacancy with steady hours and pay sufficient for our household bills; I won't assume a vacancy exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage gap at 63, with time to look and some local options. I am not choosing to retire before the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children we are checking our own income first, not asking them to support us. They have households of their own, and I want any decision based on actual statements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes an inspection vacancy workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a real local posting, a wage that meets our bills and hours I can work safely. A short invited talk about inspections would not be a paid job.

say: **2028 thinking AI** plans door work before robots fit frames around 2031.
The contractor should publish **paid crew numbers** before shifts change.
think: At about **63**, I might lose door wages before my hoped-for exit at 66.
Three months of **savings** may not bridge a long gap, even with some local jobs.
do: **Ask** contractor for fire-door crew plan and paid training options.
**Review** retirement statements with partner against bills.
**Apply** after shifts cut to posted local inspection job with bill-covering pay and safe hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage gap before affordable retirement.
S2.quote: Three months of savings and some local jobs may not bridge a fire-door wage gap to an affordable retirement.
fieldNote: Her **job move** requires an actual shift cut and a posted local inspection role with adequate pay and safe hours.
A retirement review is **information gathering**; she does not claim early exit or a guaranteed pension amount.

steps.text: Ask contractor for fire-door crew plan and paid training options
Review retirement statements with partner against household bills
Apply after cuts to posted local inspection job with bill-covering pay and safe hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 could prepare door schedules, and robots around 2034 could fit them. Five years gives the firm time to test fire safety with a real door and tell older workers what paid roles remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 66 when robots can handle the physical fitting, around the age I hope to finish regular site work. If our retirement statements cover the bills, I may stop climbing site stairs then; if they don't, I will need paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will review our retirement income and bills each year. I'll ask the contractor about funded fire-door inspection training with paid class days; if an actual place and full wages are offered, I'll enrol, and if we still need income after door shifts are cut, I'll apply to posted local inspection roles with pay and safe hours that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possibility that the income figures fall short when site robots arrive. Five years lets me seek written terms rather than guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a fire-door robot trial prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot trial must close a real fire door against the actual threshold and test the latch repeatedly. A door that looks square in a drawing may still drag when smoke protection matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes inspection training possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the course fee paid, wages through every class day and a recognised certificate. If there is no real place, I'll keep fitting doors and checking local posts rather than count an enquiry as training.

say: **2031 thinking AI** makes schedules before robots fit fire doors around 2034.
A **real closure test** and written paid-role plan matter before the site changes.
think: At about **66**, planned retirement works only if statements cover bills.
If the figures fall short, I still need **paid inspection work** with safe hours.
do: **Review** retirement income and bills with partner each year.
**Enrol** in recognised inspection course if fees, real place and full class wages secured.
**Apply** after door cuts if income needed to posted local inspection job with bill-covering pay and safe hours.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement figures falling short as robots arrive.
S3.quote: A door that looks square in a drawing may still drag when smoke protection matters.
fieldNote: Her possible exit at **66 remains conditional** on actual household income; there is no automatic retirement decision.
Training requires **funded fees**, full wages and a real place; later posted local work must have safe hours and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Review retirement income and household bills with partner yearly
Enrol in recognised inspection course if fees, real place and full class wages secured
Apply after door cuts if income needed to posted local inspection job with bill-covering safe hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may make the schedules, then robots around 2039 may fit the doors. I hope to have stopped regular site work around 66 if our money supports it, so the next crew needs the safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 71 when robots do the fitting, beyond my hoped-for working years. We cannot guarantee a retirement date today, but the longer runway lets us see the statements and plan a careful handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting and testing doors now, while I am on the site rota, and review our retirement figures each year. Before I leave regular work, if the finances allow it, I'll walk the younger fitter through the closer test and leave measured notes for each apartment floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about whether the income will be enough to stop at 66, but less worried about a robot arriving when I would be 71. The handover feels doable with time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety check would you pass on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the younger fitter how the latch catches after the closer pulls the door through the last few inches. A fire door is not safe because the checklist says closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the handover useful after you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notes would list the floor, door number, hinge adjustment and result of the closing test. I'd walk one finished floor with the younger fitter before leaving, not claim to be working there in 2039.

say: **2036 thinking AI** precedes fire-door robots around 2039.
Younger fitters need **closer tests** and measured notes before older workers leave.
think: At about **71**, robots likely arrive after my hoped-for exit at 66.
Retirement remains **conditional on income**, not an assumption that site wages can stop today.
do: **Keep** fitting and testing fire doors while on current site rota.
**Review** retirement income with partner each year.
**Walk** younger fitter through closer test before leaving if finances support exit.
feel: **Uneasy** about retirement affordability, with time for a careful handover.
S4.quote: A fire door is not safe because the checklist says closed.
fieldNote: She separates **current site work** from a conditional handover before exit, without claiming employment at 71.
Her three-month reserve makes **retirement affordability** a live question even when robots arrive beyond the hoped-for work period.

steps.text: Keep fitting and testing fire doors on current site rota
Review retirement income with partner yearly
Walk younger fitter through closer test before exit if finances allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could reduce door shifts when I would be about 63, before the age I hope to stop. A written paid-role plan, funded inspection training and actual local vacancies would help if our income figures fall short.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tests the door after a robot hangs it and before people move into the flat. A fire-door checklist can be complete while the latch still misses its keeper. I want that last physical test on the handover sheet.

headlineQuote: A fire-door checklist can be complete while the latch still misses its keeper.
portrait: **Vera**, 58, is an experienced apartment-site fire-door fitter with a vocational trade certificate and typical trade pay.
Her shop-worker partner and grown children share a **three-month reserve**; some nearby contractors offer alternatives.
She uses **AI occasionally**, prefers a proven tool and hopes to stop regular site work around 66 if income allows.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about a wage gap before 66; slower change allows a conditional retirement review and handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring fire-door robots around 2031, when she would be about 63 and may still need wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **written paid-role plan**, funded inspection training and actual local vacancies would help if retirement income falls short.
